transcript.text: Dropped a cast iron pan on my ceramic hob and there's a crack right across the front left ring. It still heats up. Can I keep using it until I get a new one?

I'm afraid the honest answer is no. Please stop using it now, even though it still heats. The glass is the only barrier between your pans and the live elements and wiring underneath. Once it's cracked, any spill, steam or wiping water can get through to live parts, which is a real electric shock risk. The crack can also spread or the glass can break apart when it heats and cools, and a crack right across the ring is the worst place for that. What to do now:
1. Switch the hob off at the cooker isolator. This is usually a large switch on the wall near the cooker, often red. If there isn't one, switch off its circuit breaker in the consumer unit. That way nobody can turn a ring on by accident.
2. Let it cool fully if it's been used recently, then leave the surface alone. Don't wipe it with a wet cloth and don't put pans on it, even ones that are switched off.
3. If any glass edges are lifting or loose, wear gloves if you need to touch them, and keep children away from it. Looking ahead, the fix is either a new glass top or a new hob. On many ceramic hobs the glass isn't sold as a separate spare, so replacing the whole hob is often the outcome. It's worth knowing what yours is before you decide anything. One quick question: is this a separate built-in hob, or the top of a freestanding cooker with an oven underneath? If it's a cooker, the oven usually shares the same supply, and I'll tell you whether it's reasonable to keep using the oven while the top is cracked.

Ok, I'll switch it off. It's a separate built-in hob, with the oven underneath in the cupboard. There's a red switch on the wall labelled cooker, so I can use that. Some pasta water spilled earlier and might have gone into the crack.

Water near the plug or socket is dangerous. Please don't touch the plug, socket or machine if they or your hands are wet. If you can do it safely, switch off the circuit at the consumer unit (fuse box), keep away from the water, and don't use the machine again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has checked it. The cause is clear: the cast iron pan cracked the glass. The spilled pasta water makes it more urgent, because if any went through the crack it could be sitting on the element or wiring underneath. Because of that, the hob mustn't be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it, even if it dries out and seems fine. What to do now, all with it switched off:
1. Turn off the red cooker switch. Then also switch off the cooker circuit at the consumer unit (fuse box), because water may have reached live parts. Don't touch any plug, socket or switch if your hands or the area around it are wet.
2. Leave the hob to cool fully. Then gently soak up any water still on the surface with dry kitchen roll, without pressing on the crack. Wear gloves if any edges are lifting. Don't wipe it with a wet cloth.
3. Open the cupboard and look at the oven and the area just under the hob for drips or damp. If there's water below, keep the oven off too until the engineer has looked. That would mean water has gone right through.
4. If a breaker or RCD in the fuse box has already tripped, leave it off. That's a strong sign water has reached something live. As for the oven, it depends on how it's wired. If the cooker switch powers both the hob and the oven, keep both off until the engineer has checked, since they share the same supply. The cracked top doesn't affect the oven itself. When the engineer comes, the realistic outcome is either a new glass top, if one is available for your hob, or a replacement hob. Replacing the whole hob is often the answer on ceramic models. So, does the red cooker switch turn off the oven as well, or is the oven plugged in separately?
I'm not sure whether the red cooker switch also turns off the oven. I can't tell from here. There was no trip, smell or sparking, and I'll switch the hob off now.

No trip, smell or sparking is good news. It means nothing has obviously shorted so far. It doesn't clear the hob, though. Water that got into the crack can sit on the element or wiring and cause a problem later, and the glass itself is still broken. So the hob stays off until an engineer has checked it, whatever happens next. You don't need to work out the wiring to find out about the oven. You can see it for yourself:
1. Turn off the red cooker switch, then look at the oven's clock or display. If it goes blank, the oven runs from the same supply as the hob, and switching off the cooker switch has made both safe.
2. If the clock stays lit, the oven is on its own supply, probably a plug or a separate switch. Then switch off the cooker circuit at the fuse box as well. Check the clock again: if it's still on, the oven is most likely wired separately from the hob.
3. With everything off, look under the hob in the cupboard and on top of the oven for damp or drips. Use a torch if needed and don't touch any wiring. If the oven turns out to be on a separate supply and everything under the hob is completely dry, using the oven while you wait is reasonable. The crack is in the hob, not the oven. If there's any damp underneath, or the oven shares the hob's supply, leave both off until the engineer has been. When you book the engineer, mention the dropped pan, the crack across the ring and the pasta water. They'll check for water inside and tell you whether a replacement glass top exists for your hob or whether a new hob makes more sense. Is there any sign of damp under the hob or on the oven?
I've not looked yet. I'll switch the cooker switch off and check the oven clock, but I can't get to the cupboard under the hob to look because the oven is built in beneath it. Is that okay?

Yes, that's fine. Please don't try to get under there. With the oven built in beneath the hob, the only way to reach that space is to pull the oven out, and that's a job for the engineer. It does change one thing I said earlier. I suggested the oven might be OK to use if it was on its own supply and everything underneath was dry. Because nobody can confirm it's dry, the cautious answer now is to leave the oven off too until the engineer has been. Water from the crack would drip straight down towards the top of the oven, so it's the appliance most at risk. What's still useful to do, all with everything switched off:
1. Turn off the red cooker switch and look at the oven clock. If it goes blank, one switch controls both, so the engineer only needs to isolate one circuit.
2. If the clock stays lit, the oven is on a separate supply. Switch it off there as well (its own switch or the fuse box), so neither appliance can be used by accident.
3. Without touching anything, look along the gap between the front edge of the hob and the top of the oven, using a torch if it helps. Any drips or water marks there would mean water has most likely gone through. Tell the engineer if you see any. Seeing none doesn't clear it, though, because water could be sitting further back. The hob itself stays out of use whatever you find, until a qualified engineer has checked it. When you book, mention that the oven is built in underneath. They'll need to pull it out to check for water and to replace the hob or its glass, so they'll plan the job with that in mind. When you turn the cooker switch off, does the oven clock go blank or stay lit?
I haven't switched it off and checked the clock yet, I'll do that now. I can't see into the gap very well from here though, so I'm not sure I'll be able to tell if there's any damp. Is that ok?

Yes, that's absolutely fine. Please don't lean in, use a mirror on a stick or poke anything into that gap to get a better look. It was only ever a bonus check, and it couldn't have cleared the hob anyway, because water could be sitting further back where nobody can see it from the front. So not being able to see changes nothing about what happens next. The hob stays off. The oven stays off too until an engineer has pulled it out and checked underneath. That's their job, not yours. The one thing still worth doing is the clock check you're about to do:
1. Turn off the red cooker switch and watch the oven clock.
2. If it goes blank, that one switch isolates both the hob and the oven. Leave it off.
3. If it stays lit, the oven has its own supply. Switch that off too, either at its own switch or at the fuse box, so nobody uses it by accident while you wait. Either way, it's a useful detail to pass on when you book the engineer, along with the dropped pan, the crack across the front left ring, the pasta water, and the fact that the oven is built in underneath. With that information they can come prepared to take the oven out. They can then tell you whether a replacement glass top is available for your hob or whether a new hob is the more sensible fix. If you'd like, let me know what the clock does and I'll help you work out what to ask them.
